title: Act I, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: At a camp near Forres a bleeding Captain tells Duncan how 'brave Macbeth' cut the rebel Macdonwald open 'from the nave to the chaps' and, with Banquo, fought on against a fresh Norwegian attack. Ross reports the treachery of the Thane of Cawdor and the victory over Norway. Duncan orders Cawdor's execution and gives his title to Macbeth.

significance: We hear of Macbeth before we see him: a loyal, almost superhuman killer. The scene's dramatic irony is that the title of a traitor passes to the next traitor.

In “Act I, Scene II,” how does Shakespeare show Macbeth's reputation as a warrior? writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene II, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene II develops the idea of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene II suggests about Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's imagery and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses imagery in Act I, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene II and its treatment of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's imagery and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about Macbeth's reputation as a warrior in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: kingship and order
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Rightful kingship (Duncan, Edward, Malcolm) is tied to natural order; tyranny to disorder. In this scene: “fought / ’Gainst my captivity. Hail, brave friend! / Say to the king the knowledge of the broil / As thou didst leave it” (Act I, Scene II, Malcolm (speech 2)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: blood
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Blood begins as a sign of valour and becomes the mark of guilt that cannot be washed away. In this scene: “What bloody man is that? He can report, / As seemeth by his plight” (Act I, Scene II, Duncan (speech 1)).

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
